topics: 📜 Never Take a Verbal Analogy Lightly — four foundational halakhot (piggul, notar, forbidden daughter, stoning) rest entirely on gezeirah shava
🫗 Blending and Applying the Anointing Oil — who is liable, who is exempt, and why oil and incense differ on 'halves'
✨ The Miracle of the Twelve Log — how Moses's small batch of anointing oil anointed the Tabernacle, priests, and kings for centuries
👑 Which Kings Were Anointed? — the House of David needs anointing only amid dispute; the kings of Israel never use the sacred oil
😟 Moses and Aaron's Worry — did the extra oil pooling in Aaron's beard constitute misuse of consecrated property?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Legal Analogy to the History of the Sacred Oil
overview.subtitle: Keritot 5a–5b
overview.hebrewSource: אַל תְּהִי גְּזֵירָה שָׁוָה קַלָּה בְּעֵינֶיךָ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: After closing out the discussion of lashes for general prohibitions (bread, parched grain, and fresh stalks before the omer), the Gemara pauses to stress how much halakhic weight can rest on a single verbal analogy (gezeirah shava): karet for piggul, for notar, for a daughter born of rape, and stoning for those liable to it are all derived this way. The daf then returns to the mishna's case of the anointing oil, detailing who is liable for blending or applying it and why blending it in partial amounts is only sometimes permitted. A lengthy aggadic excursus follows on the miracles that let the original twelve log of oil anoint the Tabernacle, priests, and kings across the generations, which kings of the house of David were anointed and why, and the touching story of Moses's and Aaron's worry that they had misused consecrated oil.

slides.title: 📜 Never Take a Verbal Analogy Lightly
slides.subtitle: Four Sages each cite a foundational halakha that rests entirely on a gezeirah shava
headers: Halakha derived only by verbal analogy
rows: Karet for piggul is derived from the karet stated for notar, via the shared phrase 'shall bear his iniquity'
Karet for notar itself is derived from a second gezeirah shava, linking 'sacred' (קֹדֶשׁ) in Leviticus to 'sacred' in Exodus
Karet for intercourse with one's daughter born of rape is derived from the word 'henna' (הֵנָּה) shared between two verses about granddaughters
Death by stoning for those liable to it in cases of forbidden relations is derived from 'their blood shall be upon them,' shared with the necromancer and sorcerer

callout.label: The lesson:
callout.text: A gezeirah shava may look like a minor technical tool, but entire halakhot with no other textual basis depend on it.

slides.title: 🫗 Blending and Applying the Anointing Oil
slides.subtitle: A baraita defines exactly who becomes liable

steps.content: 1️⃣ Blending the oil to learn how it is made, or to prepare it for communal Temple use — exempt
2️⃣ Blending the oil in order to apply it to one's own skin — liable
3️⃣ Applying oil that someone else blended (not the original Mosaic formula) — exempt, since liability requires Moses's own oil specifically

4️⃣ Blending only half the specified amount: for the anointing oil this is exempt ('like it' implies the full exact composition); for the incense, by contrast, even a half-batch is liable, since incense is routinely burned in two half-portions (morning and afternoon)

callout.label: Precision matters:
callout.text: A baraita even specifies the exact weights — myrrh, cassia, and cinnamon at 500 shekels each, calamus at 250 — totaling 1,750 shekels, with each ingredient weighed independently rather than balanced against another.

slides.title: ✨ The Miracle of the Twelve Log
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehuda: many miracles accompanied the anointing oil from beginning to end
slides.hebrewSource: שֶׁמֶן מִשְׁחַת קֹדֶשׁ יִהְיֶה זֶה לִי לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם
slides.label: The account:
slides.text: Moses prepared only twelve log of anointing oil in the wilderness — despite absorption by the cooking pot, by the spice roots, and loss to the fire — and that same amount anointed the Tabernacle and its vessels, Aaron and his sons throughout the seven days of inauguration, and every High Priest and king afterward, yet remains intact for future use. Rabbi Yehuda finds this hinted in the word 'zeh' ('this'), whose gematria is twelve. The oil was later sequestered together with the Ark, the jar of manna, and Aaron's staff — a linkage the Gemara derives through three separate verbal analogies on the words 'there,' 'generations,' and 'kept.'

slides.title: 👑 Which Kings Were Anointed?
slides.subtitle: Anointing confirms a contested succession, not a routine one

boxes.title: House of David — anointed only amid dispute
items: Solomon: due to Adonijah's rival claim to the throne
Joash: due to the usurper Athaliah
Jehoahaz: due to competition from his older brother Jehoiakim

boxes.title: Kings of Israel — never anointed with the sacred oil
items: Jehu was anointed by Elisha only due to his rebellion against Joram
But the oil used was pure balsam, not the sacred anointing oil — since Israelite kings never qualify for the real thing
By the time of Jehoahaz the sacred oil had already been sequestered with the Ark, manna, and Aaron's staff — confirming only balsam was used even for Davidic kings anointed after that point

callout.label: The rule:
callout.text: A king inherits the throne without need for anointing — Deuteronomy 17:20 ('he and his sons') teaches succession is automatic — except where a dispute requires public confirmation.

slides.title: 😟 Moses and Aaron's Worry
slides.subtitle: Did the oil overflowing onto Aaron's beard count as misuse of consecrated property?

lines.speaker: Scene
lines.text: Two drops of anointing oil, shaped like pearls, hung miraculously in Aaron's beard whenever he spoke, never falling — evidence of extra oil poured beyond what was needed.

lines.speaker: Moses
lines.text: Worried: perhaps I misused consecrated property, God forbid, by pouring more oil than necessary.

lines.speaker: Bat kol
lines.text: 'Like the dew of Hermon that comes down upon the mountains of Zion' (Ps. 133:3) — just as dew is not subject to misuse, the oil on Aaron's beard was not consecrated property misused.

lines.speaker: Aaron
lines.text: Still worried: perhaps Moses did not misuse it, but I did — since I am the one benefiting from the extra oil on my own body.

lines.speaker: Bat kol
lines.text: 'How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together' (Ps. 133:1) — just as Moses did not misuse it, neither did you.

callout.label: Also disputed:
callout.text: Tanna'im disagree whether pouring oil on the High Priest's head or anointing between his eyelashes came first, and kings were anointed in the shape of a crown while priests in the shape of the Greek letter chi (Χ).

summary.principle: Small textual tools like a single gezeirah shava can carry an entire halakha, and the anointing oil — precisely measured and miraculously enduring — was reserved for consecrating the Tabernacle, the priesthood, and only those kings whose succession was genuinely disputed.

flowSteps.content: 📜 Foundational halakhot (piggul, notar, forbidden daughter, stoning) rest entirely on verbal analogies
🫗 Blending oil for oneself is liable; for the community, exempt; incense differs from oil on partial batches
✨ Twelve log of oil, preserved by miracle, anointed the Tabernacle and priesthood across generations

columns.content: 👑 Davidic kings anointed only when succession was disputed; kings of Israel never with the sacred oil
😟 Moses and Aaron each worried over the overflow oil; a bat kol reassured them both

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: precision in Torah law extends from the weight of spices to the shape of an anointing, and no analogy or worry is too small to address

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yannai, what fundamental halakha is derived only through a gezeirah shava (verbal analogy)?
o: That eating chametz on Pesach carries karet
That karet applies to piggul, derived from the karet stated for notar
That the anointing oil must be exactly 1,750 shekels
That kings must always be anointed
quiz.e: Rabbi Yannai stresses that karet for piggul — a fundamental Torah principle — is taught only through a verbal analogy to notar, showing how much can rest on this exegetical tool.

quiz.q: According to the baraita, when is one liable for blending the anointing oil?
o: Whenever any amount is blended, regardless of purpose
Only when blending it in order to apply it to one's own skin, not when learning its formula or preparing it for communal use
Only if a king personally requests it
Never — blending the oil carries no liability
quiz.e: The baraita distinguishes intent: blending to learn the formula or to supply the community is exempt, while blending specifically to apply the oil to oneself is liable.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rava, is blending only half the specified amount of anointing oil exempt, while blending half the incense is liable?
o: Because incense is cheaper to prepare
Because the oil verse says 'like it' (implying the whole exact composition), while the incense verse forbids any act of its preparation, including half-batches routinely burned morning and evening
Because only priests may blend oil
Because the two substances use different spices entirely
quiz.e: Rava explains the textual difference: the oil's prohibition ('according to its composition... like it') implies the full amount, so a half-batch is permitted; the incense's language covers any act of its preparation, including the half-portions actually burned twice daily.

quiz.q: Why were Solomon, Joash, and Jehoahaz — all kings of the house of David — anointed, when kingship is normally inherited without anointing?
o: Because all firstborn sons required anointing
Because each faced a disputed or contested succession (Adonijah, Athaliah, or an older brother's rivalry)
Because they were not sons of previous kings
Because the anointing oil needed to be used up periodically
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that anointing is required only to publicly confirm kingship when there is a dispute over succession; ordinarily, per Deuteronomy 17:20, the throne passes by inheritance without anointing.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's story, what reassured Moses and then Aaron that the extra oil pooling in Aaron's beard was not misuse of consecrated property?
o: A calculation that the amount was too small to matter
A bat kol (Divine Voice) comparing the oil to the dew of Hermon, which is not subject to misuse
A ruling from the Sanhedrin
Aaron simply wiped the oil away before it accumulated
quiz.e: A Divine Voice reassured Moses by comparing the oil on Aaron's beard to Hermon's dew, which carries no consecration, and then reassured Aaron using the verse about brothers dwelling together, since Moses himself was not liable for misuse.
